extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of social institutions / history
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter discussing the influence of religion on social morality and the legal, educational, and social position of women in the United States, comparing customs and institutions with Europe. It surveys legal rights, employment, education (including co-education), social customs, and political participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as foundation of morality and social polity
rubrics_metrics.description: History ... can tell us is that hitherto civilized society has rested on religion, and that free government has prospered best among religious peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religion is described as the chief sanction for morality and the basis of public order; in republics, where rule rests on the will of the majority rather than force, the sustaining influence of religion (reverence, self-control) is particularly important. The text contrasts possible replacement bases (custom, sympathy, perception of advantages of order) but emphasizes the historical fact that societies have relied on religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of moral/social instability from loss of religious belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Would the moral code stand unshaken, and with it the reverence for law, the sense of duty towards the community, and even towards the generations yet to come?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter raises the evaluative question: if belief in the invisible vanished, could custom, sympathy, and recognition of mutual advantage replace supernatural sanctions? It notes uncertainty (history cannot answer) but stresses that in America, rapid intellectual movements could cause significant change because of weaker visible reverences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy requires sources of reverence and self-control
rubrics_metrics.description: The more democratic republics become, the more the masses grow conscious of their own power, the more do they need to live, not only by patriotism, but by reverence and self-control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a criterion for stable republican government, the presence of social sources that produce reverence and self-restraint (often religious or analogous institutions) is presented as essential; the text implies that evaluating a republic includes assessing whether such sources exist and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of divorce frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: The great frequency of divorce in many States ... does not appear to betoken immorality, but to be due to the extreme facility with which the law allows one or both of a married pair to indulge their caprice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divorce rates are not taken as a straightforward moral indicator; evaluators should consider legal procedure and accessibility of divorce when assessing social morality. The chapter advises caution in inferring immorality from divorce statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position of women as a test of civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The position which women hold in a country is, if not a complete test, yet one of the best tests of the progress it has made in civilization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of a society's civilization should include measures of respect for women, freedom accorded to them, and their participation in public and intellectual life. The text treats women's position as a multi-faceted indicator (legal, educational, economic, social).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal equality in private rights and property control
rubrics_metrics.description: Women have been placed in an equality with men as respects all private rights ... Married as well as unmarried women have long since (and I think everywhere) obtained full control of their property, whether obtained by gift or descent, or by their own labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating women's legal status, check statutory provisions across states for equality in private rights, property control, guardianship rights over children, and whether such rights are enshrined in constitutions rather than left to ordinary legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special legal protections and labor legislation for women
rubrics_metrics.description: Special protection as respects hours of labour is given to women by the laws of many States, and a good deal of recent legislation has been passed with intent to benefit them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider presence and quality of labor protections (e.g., restricted hours) as part of assessing women's legal position; note that legislation may be well-intended but not always well-chosen in effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to professions and employment opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Women have made their way into most of the professions more largely than in Europe ... they practise as physicians ... several have secured admission to the bar ... they form an overwhelming majority of the teachers in public schools ... many are employed as clerks or secretaries ... typewriting work is largely in their hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate practical access to professions (medicine, law, ministry, teaching, clerical work, journalism) and the level of social prejudice to be overcome. Also note areas with limited entry (e.g., engineering) and regional variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public provision and equality in education for girls
rubrics_metrics.description: The public provision for the instruction of girls is quite as ample and adequate as that made for boys ... grammar schools and high schools are organized for the reception of girls ... the number of girls who continue their education in the higher branches ... is as large as, in many places larger than, that of the boys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should examine elementary through secondary provision, curricula equality (including classics and physical science), and rates of continuation into higher branches. Also consider private boarding/day schools and regional differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: University education and co-education conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: University education is provided for women ... Co-education has worked well in institutions like Antioch and Oberlin ... where manners are plain and simple, where the students all come from a class in which the intercourse of young men and young women is easy and natural, and where there is a strong religious influence pervading the life of the place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter gives conditions under which co-education is successful (social simplicity, prior ease of intercourse, religious influence). It also notes potential problems (social distractions, students' aversion in some cases) and that women's colleges continue to meet needs where co-education may be less appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social customs granting women greater personal freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom allows to women a greater measure of freedom in doing what they will and going where they please than they have in any European country ... No one is surprised to see a lady travel alone from the Atlantic to the Pacific, nor a girl of the richer class walking alone through the streets of a city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging women's social position, consider prevailing customs around mobility, unescorted travel, and public presence; note regional variation (West vs. Eastern cities) and implications for women's independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social intercourse of youths and implications for family life
rubrics_metrics.description: Social intercourse between youths and maidens is everywhere more easy and unrestrained than in England or Germany ... In the rural districts, and generally all over the West, young men and girls are permitted to walk together, drive together, go out to parties, and even to public entertainments together, without the presence of any third person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links freer pre-marital intercourse and acquaintance with larger opportunities for learning character before betrothal, attributing happier marriages in rural districts to these practices. Evaluators should weigh customs of courtship and chaperonage as factors in social outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's public and philanthropic influence vs. partisan politics
rubrics_metrics.description: American women take far less part in politics than their English sisters, although more than the women of Germany, France, or Italy. ... They have long borne a conspicuous part in the promotion of moral and philanthropic causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess women's civic influence both in formal political participation (voting, holding offices, party activity) and in philanthropic/ reform movements (temperance, charity organization, education). Note that suffrage, where granted, carries with it rights to offices.
